title: Retest Day: What Your New the average skinny guy Number Proves About Your benchmark data
description: Retest day against the most honest benchmark of all: the average skinny guy. Today your new dead hang time gets placed in the data. What does your number prove about your tendons compared to men built exactly like you? Bring your day-one time.

scenes.narration: Retest day, honest edition. | Ninety days ago | your dead hang | was compared to nothing. | Today it meets the average. | Same bar as day one. | Same overhand grip. | Same chalk rules, frozen. | Jump up and settle. | Shoulders packed down. | Body quiet, breath slow. | No swinging. | No re-gripping. | No kicking for seconds. | When your fingers open, | the clock stops. | That is your NEW time. | Got it? | At the end, | I place it | against the average | skinny guy's hang | and read what it proves.

scenes.label: WHAT THE AVERAGE SKINNY GUY HANGS
scenes.sub: most untrained light men stop under 30 seconds
scenes.narration: Here is the benchmark nobody quotes, because it is not flattering to anyone. When researchers and coaches test untrained young men of light build, the typical dead hang lands under thirty seconds, and plenty stop near twenty. Not because skinny men have weak tendons by birth, but because nothing in modern light-framed life ever asks the grip to hold the whole body. Desks do not test it. Phones do not train it. So the average skinny guy's hang is not a genetic verdict. It is a measurement of an untested system. Your day-one time probably lived right there in that average, which is exactly what makes today's placement worth reading.

Look at what separates you from that average now, inside the forearm. The average skinny guy's flexor tendons have spent years transmitting typing-level forces. They are healthy, normal, and completely unprepared for bodyweight tension, so his fingers open early from a mixture of soft transmission and alarm. Ninety days of hanging rebuilt your transmission: collagen aligned along the pull, stiffness up, and a nervous system that stopped treating bodyweight as an emergency. Same build, same bones, same starting equipment. The difference between the average and you is not the hardware you were issued. It is the loading history written into identical hardware. One more detail in the average data is quietly on your side. The average skinny guy's hang fails early partly because his grip has never been asked a hard question, but also because his shoulders have never learned to pack under load, and unpracticed shoulders end hangs before grips do. Which means the average is beatable at two separate points, and your ninety days trained both of them. When you read your distance from the average, remember it is a distance measured across two systems, not one, and you improved both.

Now read the placement like a scientist. There are two distances to measure today. Your distance from your day-one self, which is the training story. And your distance from the current average, which is the standing story. They answer different questions. The first tells you whether the work worked. The second tells you what the work is worth in a world of men built like you who did not do it. A man at sixty seconds stands roughly two average skinny guys tall on this test. At ninety, he is an outlier his own build category cannot explain without mentioning his training, which is the finest compliment benchmark data can pay. One more distance in the data is worth measuring while you are here. Compare your hang not only to the untrained average but to the trained averages for your build, the numbers posted by men a season or two ahead of you. That is your realistic horizon: not a heavyweight's time, not a gymnast's, but the next ring of your own category. Benchmarks work best as a ladder of near neighbors. The average tells you where you escaped from. The next ring tells you where supper is.

beats.text: AN OUTLIER IN YOUR OWN BUILD

scenes.narration: One more thing the data quietly proves, and it matters for how you train next. The average is not static. Untrained systems drift downward with age and disuse, so the average skinny guy of thirty-five hangs less than the average of twenty-five, who hangs less than he could have at any point he chose to start. Standing still relative to the average actually requires improving, slowly, forever, because the average itself is sinking. Your ninety days did not just lift you above the line. They changed your relationship to it: you are now a man whose number rises on purpose while the line sinks by default. And the shoulders' half of the average deserves a fair hearing in the verdict. When the average skinny guy's hang ends at twenty-five seconds, post-mortems usually blame his fingers, but slow-motion honesty shows the shoulders surrendering first in a large share of cases: the shrug creeps in, the joint unpacks, and the fingers inherit an impossible job. Your ninety days trained the pack until it became reflex. Part of your distance from the average is a shoulder story, and it will keep paying you in every hang, pull, and carry you ever do.

The reframe for average day is the mission statement of this channel. Skinny was never the disadvantage in this test. Untrained was. The average skinny guy and the trained skinny guy share a skeleton and differ by a season of hangs, which means the entire gap between average and elite, for men of your build, is made of behavior. Not genetics, not budget, not equipment: a bar, a clock, and ninety days. When someone built like you says he could never hang a minute, he is not describing his tendons. He is describing his calendar, and calendars can be edited by anyone, starting today.

beats.text: A BAR, A CLOCK, A SEASON

scenes.narration: Now we hang together above the average. Four rounds of thirty seconds, thirty to reset, every round at test standard. This is the behavior the data was measuring, happening live.

Your next-season protocol depends on your placement. If you are still inside the average band, the mission is escape velocity: three hang days a week, submax sets, and the retest in thirty days, because the first band boundary is the most valuable one you will ever cross. If you are at double the average, the work becomes density and towel hangs, the stimuli that separate trained from elite. If you are at triple, your season is about defense and breadth, bringing the other systems up to where your grip already lives. The mistakes to retire: comparing yourself to heavyweight hangers as if load were equal, hiding a bad retest, and treating the average as a ceiling instead of a floor you once stood on. One weekly detail protects your distance from the average: the variety hang. Once a week, hang from something awkward: a towel over the bar, a thick branch, a doorframe edge, at honest submax effort. Averages are built on men who can only perform in perfect conditions. Trained systems perform in the world as it is, and the world rarely offers a knurled bar at perfect height. Keep the retest standard frozen. Let one weekly session be gloriously unstandardized.

scenes.label: THE AVERAGE VERDICT
scenes.sub: comment your new time and your day-one time
scenes.narration: So what does your new number prove? If it clears the average, it proves your tendons are no longer the standard-issue set your build came with; they are trained tissue on an untrained frame's skeleton, and the data cannot tell you apart from a natural. If it doubles the average, it proves behavior beat build so completely that your category needs a footnote with your name on it. If it still sits inside the band, it proves the honest distance remaining, and your day-one gap proves you are closing it at working speed. Comment both times below, and set the next placement test thirty days out. The average will be there, sinking politely. You will not be in it.

beats.text: YOU WILL NOT BE IN IT

scenes.narration: The average skinny guy is not your rival. He is your before picture, drawn by statistics. Keep hanging, keep the rules frozen, and bring me a wider distance next retest. Subscribe, because we leave averages here. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
